chapters.title: Orientation — What is Power BI and why does it exist?

lessons.title: 1. What is Power BI?
lessons.html:
• Power BI is a business intelligence (BI) tool made by Microsoft. It lets you connect to data, clean it, model it, and turn it into interactive reports and dashboards.
  • It is used by analysts, students, and companies to answer questions about their data visually — instead of staring at rows of numbers in a spreadsheet.
  • Example: a sales manager wants to know which product sells best each month, in which region, compared to last year. Power BI turns a raw Excel file into an interactive chart they can click and filter in seconds.
  • Three parts of Power BI:
    • Power BI Desktop — the Windows app where you build everything. This is what you install and use for TPs.
    • Power BI Service — a website (app.powerbi.com) where you publish and share reports.
    • Power BI Mobile — a phone app to view published reports.
  • Important: Power BI Desktop only runs on Windows. For TPs you need a Windows machine. This course teaches you the concepts and logic so you can work in the real software confidently.

lessons.title: 2. Power BI vs Excel — what's the difference?
lessons.html:
• Both tools work with data, but they are designed for different things.
  • Excel = a spreadsheet. You manually type, edit, and calculate in cells. Good for small datasets, formulas in cells, one-off calculations.
  • Power BI = a reporting engine. You connect to data (you don't edit it directly), clean it automatically, and build visual dashboards that update when the data changes.
  • Key differences:
    • Excel struggles with millions of rows. Power BI handles them easily.
    • In Excel you change the data itself. In Power BI you write transformation steps that are re-applied every time the data refreshes.
    • Power BI reports are interactive — slicers, filters, drill-down. Excel charts are mostly static.
    • Power BI has a dedicated formula language (DAX) for calculations across tables. Excel uses cell formulas.
  • When to use which: Use Excel for quick personal analysis. Use Power BI when you need recurring reports, big data, or interactive dashboards for a team.

lessons.title: 3. The Power BI workflow — 4 stages
lessons.html:
• Every Power BI project follows the same four stages. Understanding this before touching the software saves a lot of confusion.
  • Stage 1 — Connect: Tell Power BI where your data lives (a CSV file, an Excel file, a website, a database). Power BI reads it without modifying the original.
  • Stage 2 — Transform (Power Query): Clean and reshape the data before loading it. Remove junk rows, fix data types, rename columns, pivot/unpivot. This happens in the Power Query Editor.
  • Stage 3 — Model: Define relationships between tables (like linking a sales table to a products table by product ID). This is the Data Model.
  • Stage 4 — Visualize: Build charts, tables, and dashboards on the Report canvas. Add slicers so users can filter interactively.
  • Trap: Many beginners skip Stage 2 and jump straight to building charts on messy data. The chart will be wrong. Always clean first.

lessons.title: 4. The Power BI Desktop interface
lessons.html:
• When you open Power BI Desktop you see three main views, switched by icons on the left sidebar:
  • Report view (default) — the canvas where you drag visuals and build your dashboard. Most of your time is here.
  • Data view — shows your loaded tables as a spreadsheet. You can browse data and write calculated columns here.
  • Model view — shows all your tables as boxes with lines connecting them. You manage relationships here.
  • The ribbon at the top has tabs: Home, Insert, Modeling, View, Optimize, Help. Each tab shows relevant buttons.
  • The Filters pane (right side) — add filters that apply to visuals, pages, or the whole report.
  • The Visualizations pane (right side) — choose chart types and configure which fields go on which axis.
  • The Fields pane (right side) — lists all your tables and columns. Drag them onto the canvas or into visuals.
  • Key button: Transform Data in the Home ribbon — this opens the Power Query Editor where all data cleaning happens.

lessons.title: 5. What is Power Query?
lessons.html:
• Power Query is the data-preparation engine inside Power BI. It is where you clean, reshape, and transform your data before it enters the model.
  • Think of it as a recorded set of instructions. Every transformation you apply gets recorded as a step. When Power BI refreshes the data, it replays all those steps automatically.
  • Power Query has its own editor — the Power Query Editor — which opens as a separate window inside Power BI Desktop.
  • Key parts of the Power Query Editor:
    • Queries pane (left) — lists all your data sources (queries). Each imported file or table is one query.
    • Data preview (centre) — shows the current state of the data after all applied steps.
    • Applied Steps pane (right) — the list of every transformation you've done, in order. You can click any step to see what the data looked like at that point.
    • Formula bar (top) — shows the M expression for the selected step.
    • Ribbon — tabs for Home, Transform, Add Column, View.
  • Trap: Changes made in Power Query Editor are not saved to your report until you click Close & Apply. If you close without applying, your changes are lost.

lessons.title: 6. M language — a first look
lessons.html:
• Everything you do in Power Query Editor generates code in a language called M (officially: Power Query Formula Language).
  • You don't need to write M yourself at first — the UI generates it for you. But reading it helps you understand what's happening and fix errors.
  • Every M query has the same structure:
    let
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Step2 = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source),
    Step3 = Table.RemoveColumns(Step2, {"OldCol"})
in
    Step3
  • let starts the query. Each line defines a step — a name, then =, then what it does.
  • in tells Power Query which step is the final output.
  • Each step uses the previous step's result as its input. This is why step order matters — delete a step in the middle and later steps break.
  • You will see M code in the formula bar when you click a step in Applied Steps. You don't need to memorize syntax now — just understand the shape.

lessons.title: 7. DAX — a first look
lessons.html:
• DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is Power BI's calculation language. You use it to write measures and calculated columns in the data model.
  • DAX is completely separate from M. M transforms data before it loads. DAX calculates on data after it loads.
  • Simple example:
    Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])
    This measure adds up every value in the Amount column of the Sales table.
  • M vs DAX — when to use which:
    • Use M (Power Query) for cleaning, reshaping, importing — anything that changes the shape or content of the table.
    • Use DAX for calculations, aggregations, comparisons — anything that computes a value from existing columns.
  • Common beginner mistake: Creating a calculated column in DAX when a transformation in Power Query would be cleaner and faster. If you're changing data structure — use Power Query. If you're calculating a new value from existing columns — use DAX.

chapters.title: Data Fundamentals — tables, types, nulls, and messy data

lessons.title: 1. What is data?
lessons.html:
• Data = recorded facts or observations. A temperature reading, a sale amount, a student's grade, a product name — all data.
  • In Power BI, data almost always lives in tables. A table is a grid: rows going down, columns going across.
  • Row (also called a record) = one complete observation. One sale, one student, one product.
  • Column (also called a field or attribute) = one property shared by all rows. All the names, all the prices, all the dates.
  • Cell = the intersection of one row and one column. Contains one value.
  • Header = the first row of a table that names each column. Power BI needs headers to know what each column means.
  • Example — a sales table:
    OrderID | Product  | Amount | Date
1       | Laptop   | 1200   | 2024-01-15
2       | Mouse    | 25     | 2024-01-16
3       | Keyboard | 45     | 2024-01-16
    3 rows, 4 columns, 12 cells.

lessons.title: 2. Structured vs unstructured data
lessons.html:
• Structured data = data that fits neatly into rows and columns. CSV files, Excel tables, database tables. Power BI works best with structured data.
  • Unstructured data = data with no fixed format. Emails, PDFs, images, free-text comments. Power BI cannot directly analyze this.
  • Semi-structured data = has some structure but not a perfect table. JSON, XML, HTML pages. Power BI can import these but may need extra transformation.
  • Your professor's datasets are all structured — CSVs with clear rows and columns. This is the most common format in university TPs.
  • Rule of thumb: If you can open it in Excel and it looks like a table, Power BI can import it directly. If it looks like a document or a web page, it needs more work.

lessons.title: 3. Data types — what kind of value is in each column?
lessons.html:
• Every column in Power BI has a data type. The type tells Power BI how to store, display, and calculate with that column's values.
  • Text (called Whole Number, Decimal, Text, Date, etc. in the UI) — the most common types:
  • Text — letters, words, names, codes. Cannot do math on it. "Laptop", "Ahmed".
  • Whole Number — integers, no decimal point. 10, 42, -5.
  • Decimal Number — numbers with decimal points. 3.14, 19.99.
  • Date — a calendar date. 2024-01-15. Enables time-intelligence calculations in DAX.
  • Date/Time — date + time. 2024-01-15 09:30:00.
  • True/False — a boolean. Only two possible values.
  • Trap: Power BI auto-detects types on import and often gets it wrong. A column of sales amounts stored as Text cannot be summed. Always check and correct data types in Power Query before loading.

lessons.title: 4. Null values — what does empty mean?
lessons.html:
• Null = the absence of a value. Not zero, not an empty string — literally nothing. A cell that was never filled in.
  • Power BI shows nulls as null in the data preview (lowercase, grey).
  • Why nulls are a problem:
    • A SUM of a column containing nulls ignores the nulls — sometimes that's right, sometimes it's wrong.
    • A filter for a specific value will not match nulls.
    • Joining two tables on a column with nulls produces unexpected results.
  • What to do with nulls:
    • Remove rows that have nulls in critical columns.
    • Replace nulls with a default value (e.g. 0 for sales amounts, "Unknown" for names).
    • Keep them if the absence of data is itself meaningful.
  • Trap: null ≠ 0. A product with 0 sales sold nothing. A product with null sales has no data recorded — that's different.

lessons.title: 5. Duplicates and dirty data
lessons.html:
• Duplicate rows = the same record appearing more than once. If a sale is recorded twice, your total will be wrong.
  • Dirty data = data with errors, inconsistencies, or junk. The most common types:
  • Inconsistent casing: laptop, Laptop, LAPTOP — Power BI treats these as three different products.
  • Extra spaces: "Laptop" vs " Laptop" — the leading space makes them different. Use Trim in Power Query to fix.
  • Wrong data type: dates stored as text, numbers stored as text.
  • Merged fields: "Ahmed Ben Ali" in one column instead of separate First Name / Last Name columns.
  • Inconsistent formats: dates as 15/01/2024 in some rows and 2024-01-15 in others.
  • Rule: Spend 70% of your Power BI project time cleaning data. A clean model with simple visuals is worth more than a beautiful dashboard built on dirty data.

lessons.title: 6. CSV files — your most common data source
lessons.html:
• CSV = Comma-Separated Values. A plain text file where each line is a row and commas separate the columns.
  • Your professor's files are all CSVs. Example from unpivot.csv:
    Product,January,February,March,April
Laptop,10,15,12,18
Mouse,30,25,40,35
  • The first line is usually the header. Each subsequent line is one row.
  • Delimiter = the character that separates values. Usually a comma, but can be a semicolon (;) in French/European files, or a tab.
  • Trap: French Windows saves CSVs with semicolons as the delimiter (because commas are used as decimal separators in French). If your CSV looks like one giant column in Power BI, change the delimiter in the import dialog.
  • Encoding: If you see strange characters like Ã© instead of é, the file is UTF-8 but Power BI loaded it as a different encoding. Change encoding to UTF-8 in the import settings.

cards.q: What is Power BI Desktop and when do you use it?
cards.out: Power BI Desktop is the Windows application where you build reports — importing data, cleaning it in Power Query, modeling relationships, and creating visuals. You use it to author reports before publishing.
cards.why: Power BI Desktop is the authoring tool. Everything else (Service, Mobile) is for sharing and viewing.

cards.q: Name the 4 stages of a Power BI project in order.
cards.out:
1. Connect — link to data source
2. Transform — clean/reshape in Power Query
3. Model — define table relationships
4. Visualize — build charts and dashboards
cards.why: This order matters. Never skip Transform — dirty data produces wrong visuals.

cards.q: What are the three views in Power BI Desktop's left sidebar?
cards.out:
Report view — build visuals on the canvas
Data view — browse loaded tables
Model view — manage relationships between tables
cards.why: Each view serves a different stage of work. Most time is spent in Report view.

cards.q: What happens if you close the Power Query Editor without clicking 'Close & Apply'?
cards.out: Your changes are discarded — none of the transformations you made are saved to the report.
cards.why: Close & Apply is the commit step. Without it, Power Query changes are temporary.

cards.q:
Complete the M query structure:
___(1)___
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Clean = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source)
___(2)___
    Clean
cards.why: Every M query starts with 'let' (define steps) and ends with 'in StepName' (declare output).

cards.q: When should you use Power Query (M) vs DAX?
cards.out:
Power Query (M): changing the shape or content of data before it loads — cleaning, filtering, pivoting, type changes.
DAX: calculating values from already-loaded data — sums, averages, conditional calculations.
cards.why: Using DAX to do what Power Query should do bloats the model and slows performance.

cards.q: A table has 4 rows and 3 columns. How many cells? What is each row called?
cards.out:
12 cells (4 × 3).
Each row is called a record.
cards.why: Row = record = one complete observation. Column = field = one attribute shared by all records.

cards.q: List 4 Power BI data types and give one example value for each.
cards.out:
Text: 'Laptop'
Whole Number: 42
Decimal Number: 19.99
Date: 2024-01-15
cards.why: Choosing the wrong type blocks calculations. Prices as Text cannot be summed. Dates as Text lose calendar intelligence.

cards.q: What does null mean in Power BI, and how is it different from 0?
cards.out:
null = no value was recorded (absence of data).
0 = a real recorded value of zero.
SUM ignores nulls but includes zeros.
cards.why: Replacing null with 0 is wrong when missing data is not the same as zero sales.

cards.q: Name 3 types of dirty data and how to fix each in Power Query.
cards.out:
1. Inconsistent casing ('laptop' vs 'Laptop') → Transform → Capitalize Each Word
2. Extra spaces (' Laptop') → Transform → Trim
3. Wrong data type (prices as Text) → Change Type → Decimal Number
cards.why: These three issues cause wrong counts, broken relationships, and failed calculations.

cards.q: Your CSV shows all data in one column separated by semicolons. What do you change?
cards.out: Change the delimiter from comma to semicolon in the CSV import dialog (Get Data → Text/CSV → Edit → Delimiter).
cards.why: French/European CSVs use semicolons. Power BI defaults to comma. This is the most common CSV import problem.

mcq.q: What are the three products that make up Power BI?
mcq.ok: Power BI Desktop, Power BI Service, Power BI Mobile
bad: Power Query, DAX, Power Pivot
Power BI Desktop, Excel, SQL Server
Power BI Studio, Power BI Online, Power BI App
mcq.why: Power BI Desktop is the Windows authoring tool. Power BI Service is the web publishing platform. Power BI Mobile is the phone viewer.

mcq.q: What are the four stages of a Power BI project in order?
bad: Visualize → Model → Transform → Connect
Import → Clean → Report → Publish
Connect → Model → Transform → Visualize
mcq.why: You always connect to data first, then transform/clean it in Power Query, then build the data model, then create visuals. Skipping Transform is the most common beginner mistake.

mcq.q: You receive a CSV from your professor and want to remove blank rows and fix column types before building any chart. Where do you do this?
bad: The Report canvas
The Data view
The Model view
mcq.why: Power Query Editor is the dedicated data-preparation workspace. The Report canvas is for visuals, Data view for browsing loaded data, Model view for relationships.

mcq.q: What is the main advantage of Power BI over Excel for recurring reports?
mcq.ok: Transformations are saved as steps and re-applied automatically when data refreshes
bad: Power BI has more chart types
Power BI formulas are simpler than Excel formulas
Power BI works on Mac and Windows
mcq.why: Power Query records every cleaning step. When new data arrives, all steps replay automatically. In Excel you would re-do the cleaning manually every time.

mcq.q: You click 'Transform Data' in the Home ribbon. What opens?
bad: The DAX formula editor
The Model view
A new report page
mcq.why: Transform Data is the entry point to Power Query Editor, where data cleaning and reshaping happens.

mcq.q: In Power Query Editor, where do you see every transformation you have applied, in order?
mcq.ok: The Applied Steps pane (Query Settings, right side)
bad: The Formula bar
The Queries pane (left side)
The Data preview (centre)
mcq.why: Applied Steps lists every transformation as a named step. Clicking a step shows the data at that point in the transformation chain.

mcq.q: In M language, what does the 'in' keyword indicate?
mcq.code:
let
    Source = Csv.Document(...),
    Clean = Table.PromoteHeaders(Source)
in
    Clean
mcq.ok: The final step — the output that Power Query returns
bad: The first step — the data source
A loop over each row
An import statement
mcq.why: Every M query ends with 'in StepName'. That step's result is what gets loaded into the model. The 'let' block defines all the intermediate steps.

mcq.q: You need to add up all values in a Sales[Amount] column. Where do you write this and what language do you use?
mcq.ok: In the Data or Report view, using DAX: Total = SUM(Sales[Amount])
bad: In Power Query Editor, using M: Table.Sum(Source, "Amount")
In a cell on the Report canvas, using Excel syntax: =SUM(Amount)
In the Model view, using SQL: SELECT SUM(Amount) FROM Sales
mcq.why: DAX measures are written in the Data or Report view. SUM is a DAX aggregation function. M is for transformations in Power Query, not for calculations in the model.

mcq.q: In a table with 50 rows and 4 columns, how many cells are there?
mcq.why: Cells = rows × columns = 50 × 4 = 200. Each cell holds one value.

mcq.q: Power BI auto-detects a column of product prices as Text instead of Decimal Number. What is the consequence?
mcq.ok: You cannot sum or average the column — calculations will fail or return errors
bad: The column disappears from the Fields pane
Power BI automatically converts it when you use SUM
The column is hidden in the report
mcq.why: Text columns cannot be aggregated mathematically. SUM(Price) on a Text column returns an error. You must change the data type to Decimal Number in Power Query first.

mcq.q: What is the difference between null and 0 in a Sales column?
mcq.ok: null means no data was recorded; 0 means the product sold zero units
bad: They are identical — Power BI treats both as zero
null means the row should be deleted
0 is an error; null is the correct empty value
mcq.why: null = absence of data. 0 = a real recorded value of zero. Treating them the same gives wrong totals and misleading analysis.

mcq.q: Your CSV has 'laptop', 'Laptop', and 'LAPTOP' as values in the Product column. How many distinct products does Power BI see?
mcq.ok: 3 — text comparison is case-sensitive by default
bad: 1 — Power BI normalizes text automatically
2 — it ignores all-caps duplicates
It depends on the data type setting
mcq.why: Power BI treats text as case-sensitive. 'laptop', 'Laptop', and 'LAPTOP' are three different values. Use Transform → Capitalize Each Word or lowercase in Power Query to standardize.

mcq.q: You open a French CSV and all data appears in a single column separated by semicolons. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.ok: The file uses semicolons as delimiters, but Power BI defaulted to comma
bad: The file is corrupted
The encoding is wrong
Power BI cannot read French files
mcq.why: French/European CSV files use semicolons as separators because commas are used as decimal points in French notation. Change the delimiter in the CSV import dialog.

mcq.q: Which of these is an example of structured data?
mcq.ok: A CSV file with columns: OrderID, Product, Amount, Date
bad: A PDF report with paragraphs of text
An email from a client
A folder of product images
mcq.why: Structured data has a defined schema: rows and columns with consistent types. CSVs, Excel tables, and database tables are structured. PDFs, emails, and images are unstructured.

mcq.q: Which data type should you use for a column of dates like '2024-01-15'?
mcq.ok: Date — this enables time-intelligence DAX functions like year-over-year comparison
bad: Text — dates are just strings
Whole Number — dates are stored as numbers internally
Decimal Number — to allow partial days
mcq.why: Power BI's Date type understands calendar hierarchy (year, quarter, month, day) and enables time-intelligence DAX functions. Storing dates as Text loses all of this.

boards.title: Power BI in 4 steps — the full workflow

steps.say: Before touching any button in Power BI, you need to understand the four stages every project goes through. This is the map — learn it and you'll never be lost.
add: {b:Stage 1 — Connect} Link Power BI to your data: a CSV file, an Excel file, a website, a database.
{b:Stage 2 — Transform} Open Power Query Editor. Clean the data: fix types, remove blanks, rename columns, reshape.
{b:Stage 3 — Model} Define how tables relate to each other (like a sales table linked to a products table by Product ID).
{b:Stage 4 — Visualize} Drag fields onto the canvas. Choose chart types. Add slicers. Build the dashboard.

The most skipped stage:
Stage 2 — Transform.
Dirty data = wrong visuals.
Always clean before you build.

steps.say: Here's how to open each stage in the real software. Memorize where each tool lives.
add: Where to find each stage in Power BI Desktop
{b:Connect} → Home ribbon → Get Data → choose your file type
{b:Transform} → Home ribbon → Transform Data → opens Power Query Editor
{b:Model} → Left sidebar → Model view icon (third icon)
{b:Visualize} → Left sidebar → Report view icon (first icon, default)

Transform Data button
is in the Home ribbon.
This opens Power Query Editor.
Remember this — it's where
all cleaning happens.

add.q: Your professor gave you a CSV with messy column names and wrong data types. Which stage do you work in first?
add.ok: Stage 2 — Transform, in Power Query Editor
bad: Stage 4 — Visualize, fix it in the chart settings
Stage 3 — Model, change types in the relationship view
Stage 1 — Connect, re-import with different settings
add.why: Data type errors and column names are cleaned in Power Query (Stage 2). You must fix them before the data loads into the model.

steps.say: Now let's lock in the difference between M and DAX — two languages, two totally different jobs.
add: M vs DAX — two languages, different jobs
{b:M (Power Query)} runs BEFORE data loads. Changes the shape and content of tables.
{b:DAX} runs AFTER data loads. Calculates values from existing columns.

-- M example (Power Query, reshaping):
Table.RemoveColumns(Source, {"Junk"})

-- DAX example (measure, calculation):
Total Sales = SUM(Sales[Amount])

If the question is
'what does the table look like?'
→ Power Query (M).
If the question is
'what does this number equal?'
→ DAX.

add.q: You want to calculate the average sale amount per product. Which language do you use?
add.ok: DAX — write a measure: Avg Sale = AVERAGE(Sales[Amount])
bad: M — add a custom column in Power Query with the average
SQL — query the table directly
Neither — use a chart aggregation setting instead
add.why: DAX measures calculate values from loaded data. AVERAGE is a DAX function. Power Query M is for transforming the table structure, not for business calculations.

add.q: Your SUM(Sales[Amount]) measure returns an error. The most likely cause is?

The Sales table is not in the model
The column name has a space in it
